newsitem.title: UK: Banks risk big losses on options after UK budget.
newsitem.headline: Banks risk big losses on options after UK budget.

text.p: Off-exchange derivatives trades may leave Britain's leading investment banks with huge losses after corporate tax changes presented in Wednesday's UK budget, dealers said.

The immediate abolition of dividend tax credit for tax-exempt companies and pension funds has forced the issuers, or investment banks, of so-called over-the-counter (OTC) options to re-calculate the fair value of these products and reduce their risk exposure.
Call and put options give buyers the right but not obligation to buy or sell, respectively, underlying shares at a certain price, or at the strike price, at a later time.
No one knows the actual amount of risk involved or how big this OTC equity market is, but one dealer estimated potential losses up to 400 million pounds ($675 million).

"Press reports concerning the size of the risk (to banks) have been overblown and exaggerated," said one dealer, adding he believed the banks involved would have sufficient reserves to meet their liability.
"We are waiting for details in the Finance Bill on Tuesday before we can assess the true risk," he added.
Investment banks such as UBS, BZW and NatWest Markets have been said to be most at risk.
Banks use several factors in pricing an option, including the strike price, maturity, market volatility, interest rates and dividends.

Insurance companies or fund management groups offering certain long-dated investment products that guarantee a minimum return to retail customers at the end of a five-year term are the main buyers of such OTC options.

"They (the options) are usually long-dated products of five years or more," said one dealer. "Buyers of these options only go to banks with AAA or AA credit rating (which implies only a small or negligible risk of default by the issuing bank)."
These OTC options are normally linked to Britain's FTSE-100 index stock movements.
In general, higher dividends amounts paid by companies tend to lower the prices of call options but raise those of put options for the options writer, or seller.
By abolishing the 20-percent tax credit on dividend distribution, the receiver of the dividend will no longer be able to reclaim from the government the 20-percent tax imposed on dividends.
For the options writer, the lower dividend makes the price of call options higher, which benefits the buyer but makes them more of a liabilty for the issuing bank.
As a result, issuing banks were among those scrambling to buy FTSE-100 futures on Thursday to hedge against the sudden increase in risk from the OTC call options they sold.

Because the OTC contracts are long-dated and futures contracts are short-dated, banks might be forced to roll forward their futures position at a later date. As a result, dealers feared this could spark market volatility again. ($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
